name: Petit Manseng

lines.s10: Petit Manseng makes sweet Jurançon in the foothills of the Pyrenees: pineapple, apricot and honey, kept fresh by very high acidity.
lines.s20: Petit Manseng ripens late in Jurançon, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, where its small berries are left to shrivel on the vine into December. The wine is sweet with candied pineapple, apricot and honey, and its sharp acidity makes it finish clean.
lines.s45: Petit Manseng is still on the vine in December. That is the custom in Jurançon, on steep slopes below the Pyrenees in south west France. A warm, dry wind off the mountains shrivels the small, thick skinned berries, and the sugar gathers as they dry. The wine tastes of candied pineapple, apricot and honey. It is a sweet white, yet so sharp in acidity that it finishes clean. It ferments slowly, often in barrel, and no spirit is added. Bring it out with foie gras, a hard sheep's cheese or a fruit tart. They say the newborn Henri IV of France had his lips wet with a drop of Jurançon.
lines.sale: Petit Manseng is the sweet wine for people who think they dislike sweet wine: pineapple and honey, then a finish as fresh as lime. A small glass is enough, with the foie gras to begin or with an apricot tart to finish.

glass.lead: Candied pineapple, apricot and quince with honey and candied orange peel, sweet and full, cut by very high acidity.

ladder.where: Jurançon's steep slopes below the Pyrenees

glass.structure: Off dry to lusciously sweet, with some dry wines. Acidity very high at every sweetness, alcohol medium plus, body medium to full.

home.home: Jurançon, on steep south facing slopes in the Pyrenean foothills near Pau. Small, thick skinned berries hang into November and December while a warm, dry wind, the foehn, shrivels them; they are picked by hand in several passes. The sweet wine ferments slowly, often in barrel, and is never fortified. Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh grows it too.
home.abroad: Virginia has taken it up, because its thick skins and loose bunches resist rot in a humid summer; there it is made dry, off dry or sweet. The Basque Country grows a little on both sides of the border.

service.temp: 43 to 46 degrees Fahrenheit, 6 to 8 degrees Celsius for the sweet wines; a dry one a little warmer.
service.glass: A small glass and a small pour for the sweet wines; a white wine glass for a dry one.
service.decant: No. A sweet white wants only to be cold and poured small.
service.age: The sweet wines keep ten years and more; a dry one is poured within a few years.

with.why: sweetness against richness, with acidity to finish clean

with.dish: Ossau-Iraty or another hard sheep's cheese

the wine's own fruit, lifted by its acidity

labels.means: Unless it says Sec, the sweet wine of the Pyrenean foothills, from Petit and Gros Manseng.
The dry wine of the same slopes, built mostly on Gros Manseng.
Late harvest: a richer sweet Jurançon from the two Mansengs alone, picked late after shrivelling on the vine.
Sweet, in French: the style of plain Jurançon.
The white wine of the Madiran zone, dry or sweet, from the Mansengs and local grapes.

guest.a: It is usually a little less sweet, and brighter. Sauternes owes its saffron to noble rot; here the grapes simply dry on the vine, so you taste pineapple and apricot, with sharper acidity.

guest.q: The label just says Jurançon. Is it sweet or dry?
guest.a: Sweet. Plain Jurançon is the sweet wine, from gently to richly so, and the dry one says Sec on the label.

guest.q: What is the difference between Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng?
guest.a: They are two grapes of the same hills. Petit Manseng has smaller, thicker skinned berries that shrivel well, so it leads the sweet wines; Gros Manseng crops more and makes most of the dry Jurançon Sec.

compare.tell: Sémillon, as Sauternes, is waxier, with saffron and honey from noble rot and softer acidity; Petit Manseng is brighter, with pineapple and no note of rot.
Sweet Chenin Blanc from the Layon shows quince, honey and lanolin; Petit Manseng is more exotic, with candied pineapple and apricot, and sharper still.
Furmint, as Tokaji Aszú, carries the saffron and ginger of noble rot over a smoky edge; Petit Manseng shows no rot, only candied pineapple, apricot and honey.

cards.front: Petit Manseng: how does sweet Jurançon become sweet?
cards.back: By passerillage: the small, thick skinned berries hang into November and December and shrivel on the vine in the foehn, a warm, dry wind off the Pyrenees. Noble rot is not the aim, and no spirit is added.

cards.front: Why has Virginia taken up Petit Manseng?
cards.back: Its thick skins and loose bunches resist rot in hot, humid summers, and it holds high acidity at high sugar, so it is made dry, off dry or sweet.

cards.front: Petit Manseng blind: what parts sweet Jurançon from Sauternes?
cards.back: Candied pineapple and apricot with very high acidity, and no saffron from noble rot. Sauternes, from Sémillon, is waxier and softer in acidity, with saffron and honey.

questions.q: A blind white is deep gold and sweet: candied pineapple, apricot and honey, with very high acidity and none of the saffron of noble rot. Which wine is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Candied pineapple and apricot with very high acidity and no rot character point to Petit Manseng dried on the vine in Jurançon. Sauternes would show the saffron of noble rot and softer acidity.

questions.q: A guest orders a bottle labelled simply Jurançon to drink with grilled fish, expecting a dry white. What should you tell him before you open it?
opts: Plain Jurançon is sweet; the dry wine says Sec
Jurançon is a red wine made from Tannat
Jurançon is sparkling unless the label says still
Jurançon is fortified with grape spirit
questions.exp: Plain Jurançon is the sweet wine, from grapes shrivelled on the vine, and the dry one is labelled Jurançon Sec. It is white only and never fortified, so the other answers fail.

questions.q: A guest enjoys a sweet Jurançon led by Petit Manseng and asks which grape does most of the work in the dry Jurançon Sec. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Gros Manseng, larger berried and more productive, is the base of Jurançon Sec. Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon are the grapes of Bordeaux and Bergerac, not of Jurançon.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Jurançon, with Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh beside it and Virginia and the Basque Country abroad. Virginia makes a style a guest can meet there, but no New World style of it is a fixture of wine lists, so home and abroad is the right form.
The say line follows the Codex's own respelling in the South West France record, puh-TEE mahn-SENG; the Court's grid holds none for this grape.

No Codex record is contradicted. The profile, the dials and the region records for South West France, Virginia and Txakoli supplied pineapple, apricot, candied peel, quince, mango and honey, the very high acidity, passerillage and the foehn, picking by hand in several passes into November and December, the slow ferment often in barrel with no fortification, plain Jurançon sweet and the dry wine Sec on Gros Manseng, Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh, and Virginia's dry, off dry and sweet wines from thick skins and loose bunches.

The Vendanges Tardives label (the two Mansengs alone) rests on the appellation's own rule in the ministry's bulletin, read through search. Sugar floors of 40 and 55 grams a litre are given by trade sources alone and were left out.

The closing line of the forty-five second description is told as a tradition (they say): the newborn Henri IV, born at Pau in 1553, had his lips rubbed with garlic and wet with Jurançon. The regional tourism body and several general accounts tell it; historians doubt the letter of it, and accounts differ on who performed it, so the entry names no one else and no date.

The reviewed profile says honey and spice; the entry names honey and leaves the spice out, having no source that names which. Ripe peach, ripe pear, grapefruit, passion fruit and beeswax are a taster's reading beside the Codex's own pineapple, apricot, quince, mango and candied peel. The warm rung of the ladder (Virginia: ripe pineapple, mango, honey) follows the Codex's Virginia record and a taster's reading.
Whether Gros Manseng descends from Petit Manseng is proposed in the reference works and not settled, so the guest answer says only two grapes of the same hills.

Shrimp remoulade is the one dish from the Creole table, and only with an off dry bottle, as the Codex's Virginia record sends that style to spiced food. Bananas Foster was weighed and left out: the dish is sweeter than most Jurançon.
The plan's neighbours are all compared: Sémillon as Sauternes, Chenin Blanc of the Layon and Furmint as Tokaji Aszú.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after five fixes. The drying on the vine, the foehn, the late harvest rule, the tale of Henri IV and Virginia were confirmed. One guest answer was wrong (Jurançon is not as sweet as Sauternes, as a rule), and one tell denied the entry a note it lists as its own.

compare, the Furmint tell: Candied orange peel is in this entry's own lead and notes, so has none of that was not true of it; and the smoke of Aszú is Furmint's, not the rot's. Saffron and ginger are the reviewed Furmint profile.
questions[0]: The entry lists beeswax among its own notes, and wax is not a mark of rot.
cards[2].back: no saffron or wax from noble rot now reads no saffron from noble rot. The same, on the card; it still says Sauternes is waxier.
lines.s45: It is sweet, yet so sharp in acidity that it finishes clean now reads It is a sweet white, yet so sharp in acidity that it finishes clean. A guest was never told the colour. 110 words.
open: The floors of 40 and 55 grams come from a specification put to the national opposition procedure in 2014; the text now in force was not read. The entry gives no figure.

Passion fruit, grapefruit, ripe peach, ripe pear and beeswax are the author's reading; one published note gives nutmeg and clove for the spice the reviewed profile names, and the entry leaves the spice out.
Whether Gros Manseng descends from Petit Manseng is put both ways.
The opening says the grape is still on the vine in December: true of the late pickings, which is what the custom means.
